recorded: 1952, according to the source; exact session unestablished
question: What keeps a variation connected to its ground when the violin’s texture changes?
intro: A recurring harmonic framework supports chords, single-line runs and arpeggios across a D-minor–D-major–D-minor design. This is the complete Chaconne, the fifth movement of the partita, not the complete five-movement work.

cues.title: A ground beneath variation
cues.text: The opening’s broad chords establish a recurring harmonic framework in triple metre. Listen for the bass direction and the weight of the rhythm: later variations can alter almost every surface detail while preserving that underlying route.
cues.evidence: The score opens in D minor with a chordal statement, followed by variations; the four-bar ground and large minor–major–minor design are described at https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-1004. No individual chord is timestamped.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Remember the lower line
cues.text: A low note need not continue sounding for its harmonic role to remain in the ear. Across the Chaconne, try retaining the bass mentally while the violin turns to upper notes, chords or a rapid single line.
cues.evidence: This is a general guide to the written solo-violin texture, which alternates multiple stopping and single lines; the audio analysis does not separate imagined contrapuntal voices.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A manuscript dated 1720
cues.text: Bach’s manuscript of the six solo violin sonatas and partitas is dated 1720. The Chaconne follows four dances in the D-minor Partita: Allemande, Courante, Sarabande and Gigue.
cues.evidence: The autograph date and movement order are documented in the Netherlands Bach Society work account: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-1004. The date of the manuscript is not asserted as the exact composition date.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Several voices, one bow
cues.text: In the passages with several written notes together, distinguish the bass arrival from the upper line. The bow may have to distribute a chord across strings; the ear connects the resulting attacks into harmony rather than hearing an orchestral block.
cues.evidence: The score requires multiple stopping on a single violin. This is a general account of the instrumental problem, not a measured claim about Heifetz’s precise bowing at 1:48.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Variation is not decoration alone
cues.text: The score changes the rhythm, register and spacing of the harmonic framework, not merely the ornaments of one melody. Follow the recurring sense of departure and cadence even when the foreground becomes a running line.
cues.evidence: Mutopia 1426, based on the Bach-Gesellschaft 1879 score, shows the succession of chordal, quaver and semiquaver textures. This note does not assign an individual numbered variation to the timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The composer inside an ensemble
cues.text: Bach served briefly as a violinist in Weimar in 1703. His solo violin writing comes from a musician whose working life included bowed strings as well as the organ and harpsichord.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig chronology, 1703: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The surface becomes busier
cues.text: This stretch carries more frequent attacks than the opening’s chordal statements. Listen for the longer phrase underneath the small notes: increasing activity does not require a new harmonic plan at every bow stroke.
cues.evidence: The report detects roughly 4–6 attacks per second around 3:15–3:40, compared with about 1–3 in much of the opening minute. These are acoustic attack estimates, not a transcription of note values.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Chords spread across strings
cues.text: In the coming arpeggiated span, the violin distributes harmony through successive string crossings. Listen for the upper and lower edges of the chords: rapid alternation can imply several continuing lines without a second player.
cues.evidence: The score’s extended arpeggio passage begins around bar 89, estimated near 4:27. The report rises in level around 4:20–4:30 after a boundary at 4:18. This note prepares the coming texture; it does not announce an entrance at 4:12 or align a specific string crossing.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The edges of an arpeggio
cues.text: Within the broken chords, listen separately to the highest notes and then to the lowest. Their directions can create a phrase over several repetitions even when the notes in between seem to keep circling the same shape.
cues.evidence: The written arpeggio section distinguishes outer pitches while the chord spacing changes. This is a listening suggestion for the extended texture, not machine-separated melody and bass.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Two sides joined together
cues.text: The source transfer combines both sides of an RCA 45-rpm extended-play record, ERA 9544. The single digital track therefore removes a physical side change; it does not document the original session as one uninterrupted take.
cues.evidence: The upstream Archive description explicitly says “2 sides, here put together”; its photographed sleeve reads RCA ERA 9544, 45 Extended Play: https://archive.org/details/chaconne-d-moll-heifetz. The splice location and take history are unestablished.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Keep the opening in memory
cues.text: As the first minor-key span draws towards its end, remember the broad rhythm of the opening. Bach can recover its chordal weight after rapid figuration without turning the entire movement into a simple repeated section.
cues.evidence: The score recovers the opening’s broad chordal material before the change to D major at bar 133. The report shows slower attack density around 6:10–6:30 before the large 6:36 change; the note anticipates that broad recovery.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: D remains, the mode changes
cues.text: The central span turns to D major. F♯ replaces the minor third F♮, while the tonal centre remains D; the same ground can support a different harmonic colour without abandoning the movement’s foundation.
cues.evidence: The score changes key signature at bar 133. The report’s strongest boundary is 6:36, with a sharp reduction in level and a sustained shift into major-key material. The mode change is score-derived and its time is approximate, not a machine-identified chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Quietness does not remove harmony
cues.text: Across the beginning of the major-key span, compare the quieter sonority with the earlier broad chords. Harmony can remain clear through less emphatic attacks when the listener has already learned the shape of the recurring progression.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from about −14 dB before 6:35 to roughly −28 to −20 dB through 6:40–7:05, then rises. This describes the broad recorded contrast, not a particular dynamic marking.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Motion gathers within the major
cues.text: The central span develops its own faster-moving surface. Listen for the contrast between that renewed activity and the restrained beginning of the major-key section; the mode change is not a permanent instruction to remain quiet.
cues.evidence: The report’s detected attacks rise to about 5–6 per second around 7:45–8:10, after the low-density opening of the major section. No precise note grouping or tempo change is inferred.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A central crest
cues.text: The major-key span reaches a substantially stronger passage. Compare the concentrated weight here with the thin beginning of the section; one violin can make a large change of scale without adding another instrument.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 8:28 and 8:32 accompany the loudest five-second window at 8:30, about −5.8 dB. The measurement supports a local crest, not the cause of the change in bow pressure or chord voicing.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A date is not a programme
cues.text: Maria Barbara Bach died in 1720 while Bach was away with the Köthen court. The shared year has encouraged memorial readings of the Chaconne, but it does not document a commission or an intended musical portrait of her death.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv chronology documents the death in 1720. The Netherlands Bach Society presents the relation to this partita conditionally; no surviving statement by Bach establishing a memorial programme is cited.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Count the larger phrase
cues.text: Through the later major-key variations, listen for the return of a cadential goal rather than counting every small note. The recurring harmonic span remains a more useful landmark than the number of bow changes.
cues.evidence: The score’s variation design supplies the repeating harmonic framework. This is a general listening method, not an asserted bar count at 9:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Minor returns without restarting
cues.text: The return to D minor begins another group of variations, not a complete replay of the opening section. The restored minor third reconnects the later span with the beginning while its particular figuration continues the argument.
cues.evidence: The score returns to the minor key signature at bar 209. A strong report boundary at 10:18 and the lower-level, minor-key stretch after 10:15 support this approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Changing surface, familiar ground
cues.text: In the later minor-key writing, follow how a single line can imply a chord before the bow actually sounds several notes together. The alternation between implied and explicit harmony is one of the Chaconne’s principal ways of varying its scale.
cues.evidence: The score after bar 209 continues to alternate single-note figuration and multiple stopping. No particular chord or bowing is attached to this display time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A withdrawal before the close
cues.text: The later variations include a substantial withdrawal before renewed force. Keep the pulse in mind through the quieter stretch; reduced level need not mean that the harmonic progression has reached its final destination.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls to about −28 dB at 11:35, then rises to about −10 dB at 11:45–11:55. The report supports the contrast without identifying a specific cadence.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: From running line to weight
cues.text: As the ending approaches, compare the active small notes with the broad chordal rhythm remembered from the beginning. A return of rhythmic weight can announce closure as clearly as the return of a tune.
cues.evidence: The score leads from rapid figuration back to the opening rhythmic material around bar 249. Attack density rises around 12:00–12:10 and decreases thereafter; the exact start of the final thematic recovery is not bar-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening rhythm recovered
cues.text: The closing passage recovers the opening’s broad rhythm and brings the harmonic framework to rest in D minor. Its weight is now heard after the central major section and the later variations, rather than as an untested beginning.
cues.evidence: The score’s closing bars restore the opening chordal rhythm. The report shows sustained lower attack density after 12:20 and boundaries at 12:42 and 12:48; this is a broad closing-passage description, not a note-level alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The final sound remains
cues.text: The last sustained sound gives way to the recording’s residual noise and decay. Listen to the difference between the end of the musical motion and the point at which the digital track finishes.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks fall to zero by 12:55; relative level drops from −17.2 dB at 12:50 to −37.2 dB at 12:55 and −47 dB at 13:00. No exact release or noise-removal process is claimed.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

transitions.title: Chord tones become a continuous surface
transitions.how: The minor-key variations expand into an extended arpeggiated texture. Instead of repeatedly presenting a chord as a single weighted gesture, the violin spreads its notes through successive string crossings. The outer pitches still suggest bass and melody, so the new activity does not discard the harmonic ground. This is a change in how one instrument distributes the harmony, not the arrival of a new accompanying part.
transitions.evidence: The score marks the arpeggio span around bar 89, provisionally located near 4:27. The report shows a pronounced change at 4:18 followed by higher level around 4:20–4:30. These anchors support the broad transition, not the exact attack or a particular string crossing.

transitions.title: The same tonic admits a major third
transitions.how: The first minor-key span closes and the next variations retain D as tonic while replacing F♮ with F♯. Bach changes mode without changing the instrument or the underlying variation principle. The new chordal setting begins more quietly in this recording, separating the major-key span from the preceding accumulation of figuration and weight. It is a new region within the Chaconne, not a separate movement.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia/BGA score changes to D major at bar 133. The report’s strongest boundary is 6:36, where level falls sharply; subsequent material remains predominantly major. Tonal identity is established from the score, not inferred from chroma alone.

transitions.title: The third darkens while D stays fixed
transitions.how: The major-key span yields to D minor: the tonic is retained but its third returns to F♮. Bach begins another sequence of variations instead of repeating the entire opening. The change of mode restores the opening’s harmonic world while new figuration keeps the movement moving towards its final recovery of the broad chordal rhythm.
transitions.evidence: The key signature changes back at score bar 209. The report’s strong 10:18 boundary follows a level drop at 10:15 and precedes a sustained minor-key region. Exact bar timing is unestablished.

transitions.title: Broad chords recover the opening’s weight
transitions.how: The later running figures give way to the broad rhythm associated with the opening. Multiple stopping makes the harmony explicit again after passages in which a single line had implied it. The return does not start another long cycle: its cadential direction brings the D-minor framework to a close. Rhythm and chord spacing recover the beginning while their placement now gives them a closing function.
transitions.evidence: The score restores the opening rhythmic material around bar 249 before the final cadence. The 12:24 map point is a coarse score-proportion estimate within the declining attack-density passage after 12:10; no exact bar-onset claim is made.

composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
